# Jackknife and Bootstrap {#sec-resampling}

<!-- Adapted from 2025 master:06-resample.qmd at

Derivations and additional intervals are optional Supplementary reading. -->

How much would an estimate change if we collected another sample? **Jackknife and bootstrap** use the observed data to estimate its sampling uncertainty. We study both methods using one dataset, then compare their SE and bias estimates. Prediction assessment belongs to [Chapter 6](06-cross-validation.qmd); this chapter focuses on the accuracy of an estimated parameter.

By the end, you should be able to construct both kinds of resamples, calculate their SE and bias estimates with the correct formulas, and interpret a bootstrap percentile interval. The core lesson ends at [Summary](#sec-resampling-summary); derivations and additional intervals are in [Supplementary](#sec-resampling-supplement).

```{r}
#| label: resampling-setup
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, fig.align = "center",
  dpi = 160, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
rs_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(
  text = element_text(colour = "#594A63"),
  axis.text = element_text(colour = "#706477"),
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFF9F5", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFFEFC", colour = NA),
  panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#EDE4ED", linewidth = 0.3),
  plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, colour = "#635080"),
  plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, colour = "#87788F"),
  plot.title.position = "plot", plot.margin = margin(12, 15, 8, 10),
  legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank(),
  legend.key = element_rect(fill = "#FFF9F5", colour = NA))
# Small decorative friends live in the title margin, outside the data panel.
rs_friend <- function(x, y, fill, width = .043, height = .085, label = NULL) {
  grid::grid.roundrect(x, y - .005, width, height,
    r = grid::unit(2, "mm"), gp = grid::gpar(fill = "#EDE3EC", col = NA))
  grid::grid.roundrect(x, y, width, height,
    r = grid::unit(2, "mm"), gp = grid::gpar(fill = fill,
      col = "#C7B8CF", lwd = .65))
  if (!is.null(label)) grid::grid.text(label, x, y + height * .19,
    gp = grid::gpar(col = "#55445E", fontsize = 10, fontface = "bold"))
  eye_y <- y - if (is.null(label)) 0 else height * .16
  grid::grid.circle(x + c(-1, 1) * width * .17, rep(eye_y, 2),
    r = grid::unit(.35, "mm"),
    gp = grid::gpar(fill = "#6E577A", col = NA))
  angle <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 24)
  for (side in c(-1, 1)) grid::grid.polygon(
    x + side * width * .32 + width * .075 * cos(angle),
    eye_y - height * .12 + height * .04 * sin(angle),
    gp = grid::gpar(fill = "#EBA5B5", col = NA))
  u <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = 15)
  grid::grid.lines(x + width * .12 * u,
    eye_y - height * .13 - height * .07 * (1 - u^2),
    gp = grid::gpar(col = "#6E577A", lwd = .8, lineend = "round"))
}
rs_draw_plot <- function(p) {
  print(p)
  rs_friend(.932, .93, "#DAECDD")
  rs_friend(.978, .92, "#F8DCE6", width = .032, height = .065)
}

rs_school_colours <- c("#D9ECDD", "#F6D9E5", "#E3DDF6", "#F8E3CC",
  "#D8EAF5", "#F7EDC9", "#E9D6EA", "#D9EBD6", "#F8DAD3",
  "#D8E9EA", "#EADFF2", "#F6E8D5", "#E5ECCF", "#D6DFF4", "#EFD8DF")
rs_draw_samples <- function(ids, labels, title, subtitle, position_label) {
  grid::grid.newpage()
  grid::grid.rect(gp = grid::gpar(fill = "#FFF9F5", col = NA))
  grid::grid.text(title, .025, .94, just = "left",
    gp = grid::gpar(col = "#635080", fontsize = 14, fontface = "bold"))
  grid::grid.text(subtitle, .025, .865, just = "left",
    gp = grid::gpar(col = "#87788F", fontsize = 9.5))
  xs <- seq(.19, .964, length.out = nrow(ids))
  ys <- c(.72, .545, .37, .195)
  for (row in seq_len(ncol(ids))) {
    grid::grid.roundrect(.09, ys[row], .145, .10,
      r = grid::unit(3, "mm"), gp = grid::gpar(col = NA,
        fill = if (row == 1) "#E3EFE4" else "#EEE5F5"))
    grid::grid.text(labels[row], .09, ys[row],
      gp = grid::gpar(col = "#695475", fontsize = 9))
    for (j in seq_len(nrow(ids))) {
      id <- ids[j, row]
      if (is.na(id)) {
        grid::grid.roundrect(xs[j], ys[row], .044, .13,
          r = grid::unit(2, "mm"), gp = grid::gpar(fill = "#F3EFEE",
            col = "#B9ACBA", lty = "dashed", lwd = .8))
        grid::grid.text("out", xs[j], ys[row],
          gp = grid::gpar(col = "#938494", fontsize = 8))
      } else {
        rs_friend(xs[j], ys[row], rs_school_colours[id],
          width = .044, height = .13, label = id)
      }
    }
  }
  grid::grid.text(seq_len(nrow(ids)), xs, .08,
    gp = grid::gpar(col = "#8A7B92", fontsize = 8))
  grid::grid.text(position_label, .575, .03,
    gp = grid::gpar(col = "#706477", fontsize = 9))
}
```

## How Uncertain Is Our Estimate? {#sec-resampling-questions}

Last year's bootstrap example used `bootstrap::law`: average LSAT scores and average undergraduate GPA for **15 law schools**. Each row is a school, not a student. We use the usual independent-school sampling approximation for this illustration. See the [dataset documentation](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/bootstrap/bootstrap.pdf).

```{r}
#| label: resampling-law-data
# Install the data package once if needed: install.packages("bootstrap")
data(law, package = "bootstrap")
n <- nrow(law)
theta_hat <- cor(law$LSAT, law$GPA)
head(law, 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-resampling-law
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.1
#| fig-cap: "Each point is one school. The sample correlation is about 0.776. We want to estimate how much this correlation would vary across new samples of schools."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of GPA against LSAT for 15 law schools, showing a positive association and sample correlation 0.776."
rs_draw_plot(ggplot(law, aes(LSAT, GPA)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, size = 3.5, stroke = .75,
    fill = "#F3CADC", colour = "#8F729F") +
  labs(x = "School-average LSAT", y = "School-average GPA",
    title = "One sample, an uncertain estimate",
    subtitle = "15 schools | correlation = 0.776") + rs_theme)
```

Our parameter is the population correlation $\theta=\operatorname{Corr}(\mathrm{LSAT},\mathrm{GPA})$. Its observed estimate is $\hat\theta=`r sprintf("%.3f", theta_hat)`$. If we sampled another 15 schools, we would generally get a different correlation.

- **Standard error:** $\operatorname{SE}(\hat\theta)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)}$, the spread of the estimator across repeated original samples.
- **Bias:** $\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta)=\mathbb E(\hat\theta)-\theta$, its average displacement from the true parameter.

Both refer to repeated sampling from the population. We cannot observe that entire sampling process, so we estimate these quantities by systematically deleting or resampling observed rows.

## Jackknife: Leave One Observation Out {#sec-resampling-jackknife}

The **delete-one jackknife** removes each school once and recomputes the same correlation on the schools that remain. With $n=15$, there are exactly **15 replicates**, each based on **14 schools**. There are no repeated rows within a replicate and no random draws.

```{r}
#| label: fig-resampling-jackknife
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-cap: "The first three of 15 jackknife samples. An 'out' card marks the omitted school; the other 14 schools each appear once. Remove the entire LSAT/GPA pair and calculate a correlation from the retained rows."
#| fig-alt: "The original 15 pastel school cards and three jackknife samples. Samples omit school 1, 2, and 3 respectively, with an out placeholder in each omitted position. Every retained ID keeps its colour."
jack_ids <- matrix(rep(seq_len(n), 4), nrow = n)
for (i in 1:3) jack_ids[i, i + 1] <- NA_integer_
rs_draw_samples(jack_ids, c("Original", paste("Omit", 1:3)),
  "Leave one school out",
  "14 schools per jackknife sample | 15 samples in total",
  "Original school ID")
```

**The algorithm.** Start with the full-sample estimate $\hat\theta=T(D)$. For each $i=1,\ldots,n$, remove row $i$ to form $D_{(-i)}$, then calculate $\hat\theta_{(-i)}=T(D_{(-i)})$ on the retained data. Finally, summarise the $n$ estimates.

```{=latex}
\par\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
```

```{r}
#| label: resampling-jackknife
jack_theta <- numeric(n)
for (i in seq_len(n)) {
  jack_theta[i] <- cor(law$LSAT[-i], law$GPA[-i])
}
```

```{r}
#| label: resampling-jackknife-first-three
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `School omitted` = 1:3, `Schools retained` = rep(n - 1, 3),
  Correlation = jack_theta[1:3],
  `Change from full sample` = jack_theta[1:3] - theta_hat,
  check.names = FALSE), digits = 4, align = "c", row.names = FALSE)
```

```{=latex}
\end{minipage}\par
```

For example, omitting school 1 changes the correlation from **`r sprintf("%.3f", theta_hat)` to `r sprintf("%.3f", jack_theta[1])`**. This shows sensitivity to that observation; it does not establish that the school is invalid or should be discarded. Use **all 15** delete-one estimates for the following calculations.

**From deletions to SE and bias.** Let $\bar\theta_{(-\cdot)}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\hat\theta_{(-i)}$. The jackknife estimates are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}_{\mathrm{jack}}(\hat\theta)
&=\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
(\hat\theta_{(-i)}-\bar\theta_{(-\cdot)})^2},\\
\widehat{\operatorname{bias}}_{\mathrm{jack}}
&=(n-1)(\bar\theta_{(-\cdot)}-\hat\theta).
\end{aligned}
$$

```{=latex}
\par\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
```

The delete-one datasets overlap almost completely. Their raw SD measures the size of these small deletion changes; it is **not** the sampling SE of the full-sample estimator. With R's sample-SD convention, the formula above equals

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}_{\mathrm{jack}}
=\frac{n-1}{\sqrt n}\,\operatorname{sd}(\hat\theta_{(-1)},\ldots,\hat\theta_{(-n)}).
$$

```{=latex}
\end{minipage}\par
```

For the sample mean, this scaling gives exactly $s/\sqrt n$. The bias factor $n-1$ converts the small change from sample size $n$ to $n-1$ into an estimate of the leading bias at size $n$. The derivations are in [Supplementary](#sec-resampling-supplement).

```{=latex}
\par\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
```

```{r}
#| label: resampling-jackknife-accuracy
jack_mean <- mean(jack_theta)
jack_se <- sqrt((n - 1) / n * sum((jack_theta - jack_mean)^2))
jack_bias <- (n - 1) * (jack_mean - theta_hat)
jack_corrected <- theta_hat - jack_bias
```

```{r}
#| label: resampling-jackknife-results
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Summary = c("Mean of delete-one estimates", "Raw SD of delete-one estimates",
    "Jackknife SE", "Estimated bias", "Bias-corrected estimate"),
  Value = c(jack_mean, sd(jack_theta), jack_se, jack_bias, jack_corrected)),
  digits = 4, align = "c", row.names = FALSE)
```

```{=latex}
\end{minipage}\par
```

Here the raw SD is **`r sprintf("%.4f", sd(jack_theta))`**, but the jackknife SE is **`r sprintf("%.4f", jack_se)`**. The estimated bias is **`r sprintf("%.4f", jack_bias)`**; subtracting it gives the bias-corrected estimate **`r sprintf("%.4f", jack_corrected)`**. The bias estimate is small relative to the SE, so this calculation alone is not a reason to replace the original estimate.

## Bootstrap: Resample Whole Observations {#sec-resampling-bootstrap}

To estimate the sampling variability of the correlation, we would ideally collect many new samples of 15 schools and recompute it. We only have one sample. The **nonparametric bootstrap** substitutes its empirical distribution $F_n$ for the unknown population distribution $F$.

Think of putting the 15 school IDs into a bag. Draw one ID, record that school's **entire LSAT/GPA row**, return the ID to the bag, and repeat until you have 15 rows. Some schools appear more than once; others are absent. Compute one correlation, then repeat the whole process.

**The algorithm.** For $b=1,\ldots,B$:

1. Draw $n$ row indices independently, uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, **with replacement**.
2. Take those rows together as one bootstrap sample, $D^{*(b)}$.
3. Calculate the same statistic, $\hat\theta^{*(b)}=T(D^{*(b)})$.

The $B$ resulting **statistics** form the bootstrap distribution. We use its variation to approximate how $\hat\theta$ varies across fresh samples. This is a plug-in approximation, not $B$ new samples from the real population.

```{=latex}
\par\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
```

```{r}
#| label: resampling-bootstrap-loop
# Seed once, then continue the random-number stream across all B resamples.
set.seed(8670)
B <- 5000
boot_theta <- numeric(B)
first_indices <- matrix(NA_integer_, nrow = n, ncol = 3)
for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  i <- sample.int(n, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  boot_theta[b] <- cor(law$LSAT[i], law$GPA[i])
  if (b <= 3) first_indices[, b] <- i
}
```

```{=latex}
\end{minipage}\par
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-resampling-rows
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-cap: "Numbers are original school IDs, not new observations. Every row contains 15 draws. The first bootstrap sample includes school 14 four times and omits several schools; its correlation is about 0.853. Matching IDs keep the same colour. LSAT and GPA always move together."
#| fig-alt: "Four rows of 15 pastel rounded cards show school IDs 1 through 15 in the original data and the selected IDs in three bootstrap samples. Repeated and missing IDs are visible."
rs_ids <- cbind(seq_len(n), first_indices)
rs_draw_samples(rs_ids, c("Original", paste("Resample", 1:3)),
  "Same schools, fresh samples",
  "15 whole rows per sample | with replacement",
  "Draw position within a sample")
```

```{r}
#| label: resampling-first-three
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(Resample = 1:3,
  `Distinct schools` = apply(first_indices, 2, function(i) length(unique(i))),
  Correlation = boot_theta[1:3], check.names = FALSE),
  digits = 3, align = "c", row.names = FALSE)
```

**Why replacement?** Sampling all 15 rows without replacement only rearranges the same data, so every correlation would equal `r sprintf("%.3f", theta_hat)` and the estimated SE would be zero. **Why whole rows?** Resampling LSAT and GPA separately breaks the observed pairing and destroys the association we want to study.

Each row has probability $1/n$ on a draw. If several rows share a value, its total probability includes all of those rows. The bootstrap does not make distinct observed values equally likely.

```{=latex}
\clearpage
```

## From the Replicates to SE, Bias, and a Confidence Interval {#sec-resampling-accuracy}

Let $\bar\theta^*=B^{-1}\sum_{b=1}^B\hat\theta^{*(b)}$. Two summaries answer different questions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}_{\mathrm{boot}}(\hat\theta)
&=\sqrt{\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_{b=1}^B
(\hat\theta^{*(b)}-\bar\theta^*)^2},\\
\widehat{\operatorname{bias}}_{\mathrm{boot}}
&=\bar\theta^*-\hat\theta.
\end{aligned}
$$

The **SE** describes the spread of the estimator across hypothetical samples. The **bias estimate** compares the bootstrap centre with the original estimate, which plays the population-parameter role under $F_n$.

```{r}
#| label: resampling-accuracy-results
boot_se <- sd(boot_theta)
boot_bias <- mean(boot_theta) - theta_hat
percentile_ci <- quantile(boot_theta, c(.025, .975))
```

```{r}
#| label: resampling-accuracy-table
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Summary = c("Observed correlation", "Bootstrap mean", "Bootstrap SE",
    "Estimated bias", "Percentile lower limit", "Percentile upper limit"),
  Value = c(theta_hat, mean(boot_theta), boot_se, boot_bias, percentile_ci)),
  digits = 3, align = "c", row.names = FALSE)
```

Here the estimated SE is **`r sprintf("%.3f", boot_se)`**, while estimated bias is **`r sprintf("%.3f", boot_bias)`**. The estimated bias is small relative to the spread; this alone is not a reason to replace the observed correlation with a bias-corrected estimate.

**A percentile interval.** Take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap statistics:

$$
\mathrm{CI}_{\mathrm{perc}}=
\left[q^*_{0.025},\ q^*_{0.975}\right].
$$

For these data, the nominal 95% percentile interval is **[`r sprintf("%.3f", percentile_ci[1])`, `r sprintf("%.3f", percentile_ci[2])`]**. It follows the asymmetry of the bootstrap distribution instead of forcing equal distances on each side of $\hat\theta$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-resampling-distribution
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of 5,000 bootstrap correlations. The solid line is the observed correlation; dashed lines mark the percentile interval. The histogram describes estimator uncertainty, not the distribution of individual schools' GPA."
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of 5,000 bootstrap correlation estimates, concentrated near 0.8 with a left tail. The observed correlation is 0.776; the percentile interval runs from about 0.462 to 0.960."
rs_lines <- data.frame(Value = c(theta_hat, percentile_ci),
  Meaning = c("Observed estimate", "Percentile limits", "Percentile limits"))
rs_draw_plot(ggplot(data.frame(Correlation = boot_theta), aes(Correlation)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = .025, boundary = 0,
    fill = "#D9CDEA", colour = "#FFFEFC", linewidth = .4) +
  geom_vline(data = rs_lines, aes(xintercept = Value,
    colour = Meaning, linetype = Meaning), linewidth = .8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Observed estimate` = "#4C917E",
    `Percentile limits` = "#CC7799")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(`Observed estimate` = "solid",
    `Percentile limits` = "dashed")) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap correlation", y = "Number of resamples",
    title = "How much can our estimate vary?",
    subtitle = "5,000 bootstrap correlations | the same 15 schools") + rs_theme)
```

The data suggest a positive association between school-level averages, with substantial uncertainty about its magnitude. A nominal 95% confidence procedure aims for about 95% coverage across repeated original samples. This interval is approximate, especially with only 15 schools; it is not a 95% probability statement about the fixed parameter, a prediction interval for a new GPA, or a causal conclusion.

## Summary and Practical Choices {#sec-resampling-summary}

Both methods assess uncertainty in the **same observed correlation**, $\hat\theta=`r sprintf("%.3f", theta_hat)`$:

```{r}
#| label: resampling-method-comparison
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(Method = c("Jackknife", "Bootstrap"),
  `Estimated SE` = c(jack_se, boot_se),
  `Estimated bias` = c(jack_bias, boot_bias), check.names = FALSE),
  digits = 4, align = "c", row.names = FALSE)
```

The SE estimates are similar, and both bias estimates are small compared with their SEs. Their agreement is reassuring for this example, but does not guarantee accuracy with only 15 schools.

```{=latex}
\par\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
```

| Choice | How the data are reused | When it is useful |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Delete-one jackknife | $n$ samples of $n-1$ distinct rows. | Fast SE/bias estimates for smooth statistics. |
| Nonparametric bootstrap | $B$ samples of $n$ whole rows, with replacement. | SE/bias, distribution shape, and approximate confidence intervals. |

```{=latex}
\end{minipage}\par
```

- **Use the right formula.** Jackknife needs the deletion scaling; bootstrap SE is the SD of its $B$ statistics. Jackknife replicates are small perturbations, so their raw quantiles are not a bootstrap percentile interval.
- **Keep data size and computing effort separate.** Here $n=15$ schools, versus $B=5000$ bootstrap resamples. A larger $B$ reduces Monte Carlo noise, not sampling uncertainty. `sd(boot_theta) / sqrt(B)` estimates Monte Carlo SE of the bootstrap *mean*, not SE of the original correlation; see [Chapter 5](05-monte-carlo.qmd#sec-monte-carlo).
- **Match the method to the statistic and design.** Ordinary delete-one jackknife can fail for a non-smooth statistic such as the sample median. Bootstrap can handle many such statistics under suitable conditions, but ordinary resampling can also fail for extremes or boundary problems. Preserve whole independent units: paired measurements move together; clustered or time-dependent data need a suitable cluster or block method. Neither method repairs selection bias in the original sample.

::: {#exr-resampling-check}

## Check Your Understanding

1. Why are there 15 jackknife estimates based on 14 schools each? Why is their raw SD about 0.0394 not the reported SE?
2. A student draws all 15 schools without replacement for every bootstrap sample and gets an SE of zero. Why?
3. Another student resamples the LSAT and GPA columns independently. Which feature of the data is lost?
4. If we increase $B$ from 5,000 to 50,000, should the correlation's bootstrap SE shrink by $\sqrt{10}$?

:::

::: {#sol-resampling-check}

1. Each school is omitted once. The retained datasets overlap, so convert their deletion spread to sampling SE using $(n-1)/\sqrt n$ times their sample SD; here the result is about 0.1425.
2. Every sample contains the same paired observations; reordering them does not change the correlation.
3. The pairing within each school, and therefore its association structure.
4. No. More resamples stabilise the estimated SE and quantiles. It is the conditional Monte Carlo SE of the bootstrap mean that scales as $1/\sqrt B$; no new schools have been observed.

:::

```{=latex}
\clearpage
```

## Supplementary {#sec-resampling-supplement}

These derivations and additional intervals extend the core lesson.

### Why the Jackknife SE Scaling Works for a Mean

For $\hat\theta=\bar x$, deleting $x_i$ gives

$$
\bar x_{(-i)}=\frac{n\bar x-x_i}{n-1},\qquad
\frac1n\sum_i\bar x_{(-i)}=\bar x,\qquad
\bar x_{(-i)}-\bar x=\frac{\bar x-x_i}{n-1}.
$$

Substituting into the jackknife variance formula yields

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}_{\mathrm{jack}}^2
=\frac{n-1}{n}\sum_i\frac{(x_i-\bar x)^2}{(n-1)^2}
=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2
=\frac{s^2}{n},
$$

where $s^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2/(n-1)$. Thus the jackknife SE is exactly the usual estimate $s/\sqrt n$. This identity does not claim that an estimated SE is generally unbiased. For sufficiently smooth statistics, a first-order linear approximation motivates the same scaling.

### Why the Bias Formula Multiplies by $n-1$

Suppose the estimator's leading bias at sample size $m$ is approximately $a/m$. Then

$$
\mathbb E(\bar\theta_{(-\cdot)}-\hat\theta)
\approx\frac{a}{n-1}-\frac{a}{n}
=\frac{a}{n(n-1)}.
$$

Multiplying by $n-1$ estimates the leading bias $a/n$ of the full-sample estimator. Subtracting that estimated bias gives

$$
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{jack,bc}}
=\hat\theta-(n-1)(\bar\theta_{(-\cdot)}-\hat\theta)
=n\hat\theta-(n-1)\bar\theta_{(-\cdot)}.
$$

This is a leading-term cancellation argument for suitably regular estimators, not a universal guarantee of unbiasedness or smaller mean squared error.

### Other Bootstrap Intervals and the `boot` Package

A normal approximation uses $\hat\theta\pm1.96\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}$ when bias is negligible and the sampling distribution is approximately normal. A basic interval reflects the percentile limits around the observed estimate: $[2\hat\theta-q^*_{0.975},\ 2\hat\theta-q^*_{0.025}]$. For bounded or skewed statistics, these simple intervals can be inappropriate. Studentized and BCa intervals make further adjustments; they need additional calculations and assumptions.

The [official `boot` documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/boot/html/boot.html) describes a reusable implementation. Its statistic function must take the original data and a vector of resampled row indices:

```{r}
#| label: resampling-boot-package
#| eval: false
cor_stat <- function(data, indices) {
  cor(data$LSAT[indices], data$GPA[indices])
}
set.seed(8670)  # Independent package demonstration
result <- boot::boot(law, statistic = cor_stat, R = 5000)
boot::boot.ci(result, type = "perc")
```

This optional code performs another Monte Carlo run; its endpoints need not exactly match the manual loop. See [`boot.ci()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/boot/html/boot.ci.html) for percentile, basic, normal, studentized, and BCa intervals. A **parametric bootstrap** instead simulates new samples from a fitted probability model; its validity depends on that model.

### Sources and Further Reading

This chapter adapts the [2025 jackknife/bootstrap lecture](https://chikuang.github.io/teaching/2025F_stat8670/06-resample.html), retaining the law-school example. The [bootstrap package documentation](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/bootstrap/bootstrap.pdf) describes the dataset and its `jackknife()` implementation. Further background: Rizzo, *Statistical Computing with R*, Chapter 8, and Efron and Tibshirani, *An Introduction to the Bootstrap*.
